canDo: Can use the Mock 1 error log to pin down 3–4 recurring grammar errors (e.g. bien que + subjunctive, après que + indicative, dont/que, past participle agreement), state the rules, and use them without a single slip in a 250-word forum post.
review: Review the Day 41 error log, focusing on subjunctive triggers (bien que, à moins que, sans que, pour que), the relative pronouns dont/lequel, the contrast in mood between après que and avant que, past participle agreement with a preceding object when the auxiliary is avoir, and the difference between formal and informal register.
input: Read: a popular-science article on “mistakes and learning”, a column on automatic correction tools and a learners’ forum post; circle the structures related to your own errors as you read. Listen: an interview with a written-exam marker, a grammar column on “après que” and an ad for a media library writing workshop; note any advice you can use directly to check your own work.
output: Write: a post on a learners’ forum (250+ words) giving your view on automatic correction tools, then revise it in three rounds using the “check one type of error at a time” method; speak: a 5-minute monologue on “should spelling mistakes rule candidates out of a job?”, then a debate on “simplifying French spelling”.
checkpoint: 0 personal recurring errors in the forum post and ≤3 grammar errors overall; can explain the 3 chosen rules aloud with 2 correct example sentences each; reading and listening accuracy ≥80%; all five errors in rewriting exercise A42-2 correctly fixed.
challenge: Today’s challenge: find a grammar or writing exercise in TV5MONDE’s « Apprendre le français », then add the items you got wrong to your own “error notebook” (wrong sentence → rule → two new example sentences); redo the same exercise a week later and compare results.

questions.why: Paragraph 1 sets out the core idea: « se tromper, à condition de comprendre pourquoi, serait l’un des moyens les plus efficaces d’apprendre », and the rest covers mechanisms, conditions and methods. B is touched on only indirectly in paragraph 4; C is the opposite of the article’s point.

A mistake triggers a « signal d’erreur » that forces the brain to adjust, which « améliorent souvent la mémorisation ». A: rankings aren’t mentioned; C is the opposite: « alors même que les élèves y obtiennent de mauvais résultats ».

The second group received corrections with explanations the next day, and after a term they « commettaient nettement moins d’erreurs récurrentes ». A isn’t mentioned; B is the opposite of the finding.

Paragraph 3 sets a first condition with « Encore faut-il que… » (timely feedback), and paragraph 4 adds another with « Reste un obstacle de taille » (overcoming fear of mistakes). A: there is no contradiction; C: paragraph 4 quotes a different trainer.
« Elle recommande de distinguer clairement les moments d’entraînement… des moments d’évaluation ». B is too extreme; C is exactly what she criticises.
être coutumier de qqch = to be in the habit of, to regularly (do something), here referring to mistakes you make again and again. Neither A nor B matches the meaning.

Paragraph 2 acknowledges the tools’ benefits (« Certes… rendent de grands services »), and paragraphs 3–4 warn of the risks: a balanced position with reservations. A ignores the criticism; C: the author clearly says « Il serait absurde de les rejeter par principe ».
« Certes » marks a concession, followed by a list of three benefits. B is the opposite; C: the text gives no technical explanation.
« On clique, on accepte, on passe à la suite… sans que la règle ait jamais été intégrée ». A: the tool does make the correction every time; C isn’t mentioned.
aveugle literally means “blind”: trusting completely without judgement, even though the tool itself makes mistakes. A is the opposite; B isn’t what the word means.
The “teacher” helps us understand, while the “secretary” does the work for us; the author explains straight after: « se demander pourquoi avant de cliquer ». B and C are literal misreadings.

Mei replies to the forum topic “how to stop making the same mistakes”, describing her error-notebook method and giving advice. B: her teacher is the one who helped her spot the problem; C: she isn’t asking a question.
« sur dix copies, j’avais oublié quinze fois le subjonctif »: writing a lot didn’t mean progress. A: she writes three essays a week, which isn’t little; C isn’t mentioned.
« je la recopie, j’écris la règle avec mes propres mots et j’invente deux phrases correctes ». Neither A nor B is mentioned.
je vous l’accorde is a concession meaning “I grant you that”; here she admits the method is “not much fun”. A and C are meanings accorder can’t have in this context.
« Choisissez trois erreurs, pas plus ». A is the opposite of « ne cherchez pas à tout corriger en même temps »; C: she thinks writing more on its own doesn’t help.
The host’s first question is about the most common mistakes in B2 papers, followed by task, register, grammar and checking methods. Neither B nor C is covered.

« La première, c’est de ne pas répondre à toute la consigne », and she stresses this has nothing to do with the quality of the language. A: she says what costs most is « pas forcément des fautes de grammaire »; C isn’t mentioned.
« commencent une lettre formelle très correctement, puis glissent vers des expressions familières ». A is the wrong way round; B isn’t mentioned.
« Une erreur systématique, on peut la cibler »: a few weeks of targeted practice is enough to gain marks. B and C are guesses.
« Faites plusieurs passages courts, chacun avec un objectif ». A is exactly what she advises against; B isn’t possible in the exam and isn’t mentioned.
The whole segment is about whether « après que » takes the indicative or the subjunctive. Neither B nor C is covered.
« Par analogie avec “avant que”, qui, lui, est suivi du subjonctif ». A and C are unfounded guesses.

« “Après que”… renvoie à un fait accompli, réel, d’où l’indicatif ». A is the reason avant que takes the subjunctive; B: with the same subject he recommends the infinitive instead, which isn’t a reason for the indicative.
« après son départ » / « après être parti »: « en cas de doute, un nom ou un infinitif ! ». A is exactly the incorrect usage; C isn’t mentioned.
« il ne s’agit pas d’un service de correction : c’est vous qui réécrivez, elle vous guide ». A is explicitly ruled out; C isn’t mentioned.
« par groupes de six personnes au maximum ». « dix-huit » is the start time (18:00), a number used as a distractor.
« afin de pouvoir comparer vos erreurs d’une copie à l’autre ». Neither A nor B is mentioned.

V42-01.zh: to make the most of, to benefit from
V42-01.exZh: Good learners know how to make the most of their mistakes.

V42-02.zh: to turn the perspective around, to see things the other way
V42-02.exZh: These studies turn the perspective around: a mistake is no longer a failing but a tool.

V42-03.zh: to stick (in memory) for the long term
V42-03.exZh: A rule understood after a mistake is more likely to stick in the long term.

V42-04.exZh: Pre-tests help memory even when the results are poor.

V42-05.exZh: Leaving out the subjunctive is a recurring error in his papers.

V42-06.zh: to venture a hypothesis, to hazard a guess
V42-06.exZh: Rather than copying your neighbour’s answer, venture your own hypothesis.

V42-07.exZh: In a contract, the slightest mistake can have serious consequences.

V42-08.zh: to be prone to, to regularly make (a type of mistake)
V42-08.exZh: This candidate is prone to agreement errors.

V42-09.zh: to face up to (a problem, a fact)
V42-09.exZh: To make progress, you have to accept facing up to your weaknesses.

V42-10.zh: to be a great help, to be very useful
V42-10.exZh: This online dictionary was a great help during my studies.

V42-11.exZh: For a long time, his accent gave him a complex about speaking in meetings.

V42-12.exZh: You shouldn’t place blind trust in machine translation.

V42-13.exZh: Reading it three times takes time, but it’s the price to pay for an error-free paper.

V42-14.exZh: With or without tools, authors must stay in control of their text.

V42-15.zh: to keep a notebook (e.g. of errors, of vocabulary)
V42-15.exZh: Since September, she has kept a notebook of her mistakes.

V42-16.zh: the results are there to see
V42-16.exZh: The method is demanding, but the results are there to see: he gained four marks.

V42-17.zh: to slide into, to drift towards
V42-17.exZh: His letter starts well, then drifts into an overly casual tone.

V42-18.exZh: If I understand you correctly, rather than revising everything, I should target three errors?

V42-19.zh: to get round the difficulty, to sidestep a problem
V42-19.exZh: If you’re unsure which mood to use, sidestep the problem: use a noun.

V42-20.exZh: By analogy with avant que, many people use the subjunctive after après que.

V42-21.exZh: The decision was made without us: we were presented with a fait accompli.

V42-22.zh: (a mistake) to be picked up, to be flagged
V42-22.exZh: In the written exam, this mistake is bound to be picked up by the marker.

V42-23.exZh: The workshop teaches you to spot your own mistakes before handing in your paper.

V42-24.exZh: I write without any tools first and only open the correction software afterwards.

V42-25.zh: to level down, to lower standards
V42-25.exZh: Abolishing difficult rules amounts to lowering standards.

title: Repair day I: grammar and writing
phase: Mock exams, repair and the bridge to C1
